Eliminating Double Entry Between Time Tracking and Payroll
Every payroll cycle starts the same way for a lot of payroll administrators. Hours have already been worked. They’ve often already been approved. And now someone has to move them, by hand, into the system that actually cuts the checks.


That hand-off is where things go wrong. Not because payroll teams are careless, but because re-keying data is inherently a copy step, and copy steps introduce errors that the original data never had. When time tracking and payroll live in two separate systems that don’t talk to each other, someone becomes the connection between them. That person is doing the job a system should be doing.
What double entry actually looks like
In practice, double entry means a payroll admin pulling hours from a time clock, a spreadsheet, or a stack of paper timesheets, and typing them line by line into the payroll system. Sometimes it’s a CSV export that has to be reformatted before it will even upload. Sometimes it’s genuinely a paper timesheet a supervisor signed and handed off, with hours transcribed by hand into a screen.


Either way, the payroll system has no direct knowledge of what happened on the clock. It only knows what someone told it, after the fact, through a manual step that has to happen correctly every single pay period, for every employee, with no room for the process to skip a beat.


That’s a fragile design, and it gets more fragile as headcount grows, as more locations get added, or as more of the workforce is paid hourly. A company running one straightforward salaried office can often get away with manual re-entry for years. A multi-location employer with hourly staff, shift differentials, and overtime rules cannot absorb the same process without something eventually breaking.
The specific failure modes
Disconnected time and payroll doesn’t fail in one dramatic way. It fails in several small, mechanical ways that compound.


Transposition errors. A payroll admin re-typing hundreds of line items will occasionally swap two digits, enter 4.0 hours as 40, or apply one employee’s hours to another employee’s record. These are simple keystroke mistakes, but in payroll, a simple mistake becomes an incorrect paycheck.


Missed overtime calculations. Overtime rules depend on accurately totaling hours across a defined workweek, often across multiple shifts or locations. When hours are re-keyed from disconnected sources, the totals a payroll admin sees may not reflect the same workweek boundaries the time system used to calculate them, and overtime can be calculated on the wrong base number entirely.


Hours from the wrong pay period. Manual processes rely on someone correctly filtering which hours belong to the current pay run. If a time sheet or export includes hours that span two pay periods, or if a correction from a prior period gets mixed in with current hours, those hours can land in the wrong paycheck without anyone noticing until an employee flags it.


Approved hours that never make it into the sync. This is the quiet failure mode. A manager approves time in the time-tracking tool. But approval in that system doesn’t automatically mean the hours reached payroll. If the export or hand-off step is skipped, forgotten, or run before a late approval comes in, those hours are simply missing from the pay run, and the employee finds out on payday.


None of these require anyone to be negligent. They’re what happens when a manual step sits between two systems that should be one continuous process.
What a connected setup looks like instead
The fix isn’t a better spreadsheet template or a stricter checklist. It’s removing the hand-off entirely.


In a properly connected time-and-payroll setup, hours flow from approved timesheets directly into the payroll run. There’s no export, no reformatting, no re-typing. Once a manager approves time, that time is already in the system that will run payroll, because it’s the same system, or the same connected environment, from the start.


Exceptions get handled the same way. Instead of a payroll admin discovering a missing punch or an overtime flag during the manual re-entry process, and then reconciling that discrepancy across two separate systems, exceptions surface and get resolved inside one workflow, before the payroll run happens. That’s a meaningful shift in when problems get caught. Catching a missing punch three days before a pay run, inside the same system that will process that pay run, is a fundamentally different position than discovering it after the fact by comparing two disconnected reports.


This is the specific mechanic the pillar article “Payroll Integrations and Deductions: Making the Right Connections” describes at a category level, time-tracking software syncing employee hours with payroll calculations. What that sync actually has to accomplish, mechanically, is everything above: approved hours reaching the payroll run without a manual step, and exceptions handled once instead of reconciled twice.
Where this fits inside Asure
Asure builds toward this connected setup in two ways, depending on where a business is starting from.


AsureCentral keeps payroll, HR, and time records inside one connected system, so hours captured for a pay period are available to the payroll process without a separate export and re-entry step. For a payroll leader whose main job is getting every pay run right on schedule, that’s the difference between chasing down hours from multiple sources and working from one accurate set of numbers.


For employers with an hourly workforce, especially across multiple locations, restaurants, healthcare practices, construction crews, or field services, Asure Time and Attendance handles the capture side directly. It records punches, manages exceptions, and routes hours through manager approval so what reaches payroll is already payroll-ready, rather than a raw file someone still has to clean up.


Neither product promises payroll will run itself. What they remove is the manual copy step that turns an approved timesheet into a source of error. Hours get captured once, approved once, and used once, by the payroll process that needs them.
The bottom line for payroll and operations leaders
Double entry between time tracking and payroll isn’t a minor inconvenience. It’s a structural gap where accurate data gets corrupted on its way from the clock to the paycheck. Transposition errors, miscalculated overtime, misplaced pay-period hours, and approved-but-unsynced time are not random bad luck. They’re the predictable output of a manual hand-off repeated every pay cycle.


Closing that gap means treating time tracking and payroll as one process instead of two systems that require a person in the middle. Whether that starts with consolidating on AsureCentral or adding Asure Time and Attendance for hourly workforce capture, the goal is the same: hours move from approval to paycheck without anyone re-typing them along the way.
